newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr back from brink, but danger remains.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr back from brink, but danger remains.

text.p: The Australian dollar was back from the brink Tuesday as an impulsive offshore rally put a cent between it and Monday's 17-month lows.
The, rare, bounce came courtesy of aggressive buying of A$ against the Canadian dollar which caught a bearish market short and squeezed the currency to a two-week high of US$0.7570.

It faded there as fresh offers bloomed, and the local market was too worried today's Reserve Bank board meeting would result in a rate cut to get involved. But 75 cents was held and dealers reported growing suspicions the RBA would not ease this week which, if proved true, could see further short covering gains.
If the talk proved misguided, however, and one of these mornings did see an official cut the dollar would soon be face down at Monday's US$0.7440 floor again.
By 4.45 pm (0645 GMT) the local currency was perched at US$0.7525/30 having flown up from US$0.7453/58 late Monday.
The initial spark came from a A$300 million order against the Canadian dollar by a U.S. IMM fund which snowballed into panic buying as stops were triggered at US$0.7480 and US$0.7520.
Traders suspected funds might be switching out of C$ bonds following last week's surprise hike in Canadian interest rates, and into A$ debt where analysts saw better prospects.
Similarly there were signs of direct Japanese buying of A$ bonds this afternoon, they added, which helped extend a dollar rally to 86.65/75 yen from 85.10/20 late Monday.

Australian government bond prices have been buoyed by a very favourable inflation outlook -- underlying inflation is set to fall under the RBA's 2-3 percent target band in Q2 and Q3 -- which in turn offered the chance of yet another cut in official interest rates.
The prospect was not so welcome to A$ bulls where short term interest differentials tended to dominate and domestic money market rates had already moved below those on offer in the U.S.

The 90-day bank bill future for September stands at 94.85 implying a rate of 5.15 percent compared to the present 5.50 percent cash rate. But three month Eurodollar futures were at 94.12 reflecting market expectations U.S. rates, which are also at 5.50 percent, will be raised by September.

The Federal Reserve holds a monthly policy meeting of its own today and Wednesday, but a lack of clear inflationary signals in the U.S. has convinced most observers the Fed will leave well enough alone this time.
However, they reckon the sheer strength of the economy should force a tightening later in the year.
This contrasted with the Australian experience where the economy had proved a lot softer than expected in recent months and there were no capacity constraints on the horizon.
In this atmosphere there were few who would quibble were the RBA to ease tomorrow, which in turn made it hard for dealers to see the dollar sustaining a rally above US$0.7575 resistance.
Today's trade data added little to the policy outlook although it could be argued the persistent weakness of imports pointed to poor domestic demand.
Imports of goods fell 1.0 percent with by far the largest drop in the capital goods sector which slid 13 percent.
That was a worrying sign for business investment, said analysts, and supported the case for another policy easing.
The overall surplus of A$873 million was way above forecasts of A$163 million and the largest on record.
It was boosted by the export of a A$500 million frigate but even then analysts thought the performance good and expected net exports to make a big contribution to Q2 GDP growth.

More important from a policy point of view will be retail trade data for May on Tuesday. It was a shock 1.7 percent fall in sales for April which first started the market thinking about a fifth cut in RBA rates.

A strong bounce in sales is needed this time to stop the market looking for an immediate easing. Median forecasts are for a rise of around 2.0 percent in May and anything less than a 1.0 percent gain would be considered soft.

Also out Wednesday are building approvals data for May which should provide further confirmation of the recovery in the housiong sector. Median forecasts favour a 2.0 percent rise after a 3.6 percent gain in April.
The dollar ended at 57.4 in trade weighted terms, up from 56.7 on Monday.
